strengths: Novel and well-motivated central insight: self-attention maps in pretrained text-to-image diffusion models briefly but reliably encode instance-level boundary cues during denoising, distinct from purely semantic cross-attention or non-generative backbones (DINO/CLIP/MLLM), supported by both empirical and information-theoretic (Fisher information) justification in the appendix.

The proposed pipeline (Instance Emergence Point, Attention Boundary Divergence, one-step self-distillation, Boundary-Guided Propagation) is coherent and each component is individually ablated (Table 3), showing clear incremental contributions and confirming necessity of each part.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: unsupervised instance segmentation (VOC, COCO), weakly/tag-supervised panoptic segmentation, open-vocabulary segmentation integration, SAM seeding, and 7 additional generalization benchmarks (LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, SA-1B), plus a new instance-edge quality benchmark with ODS/OIS/clDice metrics.

Practical efficiency gains: one-step distillation reduces per-image inference from ~3.7s (inversion-based) to 45ms (~81x speedup) with negligible or even improved accuracy, addressing a key deployment concern for diffusion-based methods.

Thorough and honest limitations section (tiny objects in satellite imagery, out-of-distribution medical images) with quantitative failure-case analysis rather than cherry-picked results, which strengthens credibility.

Careful hyperparameter/metric ablations (KL vs JSD/MSE/MAE/entropy/Wasserstein for IEP and ABDiv, decoder capacity, uncertainty masking scheme, IEP stride) that convincingly justify design choices and show robustness across 5 diffusion backbones and multiple datasets/classes (Fig. 14).
weaknesses: The method has many interacting components and hyperparameters (IEP stride, KL peak selection, ABDiv neighborhood, uncertainty threshold σ, BGP IoU threshold τ_BGP); while each is ablated individually, the overall pipeline complexity may hinder reproducibility and practical adoption compared to simpler baselines.

TRACE is presented as a plug-in refinement to existing pseudo-label/UIS/WSS pipelines rather than a standalone segmentation method, so its absolute performance is always coupled with and bounded by the quality of the underlying baseline (ProMerge, MaskCut, DHR, etc.), making it harder to assess the method's stand-alone ceiling.

Reported headline numbers show some inconsistency between the abstract (+5.1 AP, +1.7 PQ) and the introduction/body (+4.4 AP, up to +7.1 PQ VOC, +16.5 PQ stuff), which could confuse readers about the paper's actual central claims and warrants clearer consolidation.

Performance varies noticeably across diffusion backbones (Table 5, AP from 6.8 with SD1.5 to 8.3 with FLUX.1), suggesting the method's benefits are partly tied to using a large, high-capacity diffusion model (SD3.5-L, 8.1B params), which raises questions about computational accessibility versus the claimed 'annotation-free' efficiency narrative.

Training the one-step distillation model still requires generating per-image teacher pseudo-edges via the full multi-step IEP/ABDiv computation across a large dataset (e.g., ImageNet, 8-10 days), which, while amortized at inference, is a non-trivial upfront cost not always foregrounded in the main comparisons.

The comparison to conventional edge detectors and depth-based instance separation methods, while informative, is somewhat narrow in scope in the main paper (deferred largely to appendix), and broader comparisons to newer/more competitive unsupervised or weakly-supervised segmentation methods beyond the selected 2023-2024 baselines could further strengthen the significance claims.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core insight that self-attention maps in pretrained text-to-image diffusion models transiently encode instance-level boundary structure during denoising, formalized via the Instance Emergence Point (IEP) and Attention Boundary Divergence (ABDiv), with a theoretical justification (Fisher information / KL argument) in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple tasks (unsupervised instance segmentation, weakly-supervised/tag-supervised panoptic segmentation, open-vocabulary segmentation, SAM-seeding) and many datasets (VOC, COCO 2014/2017, LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, SA-1B, Cityscapes, ADE20K, Pascal Context), showing consistent improvements over multiple baselines.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component (IEP, ABDiv, one-step distillation, decoder capacity, uncertainty masking, similarity-metric choice), which strengthens the causal story behind the method.
Practical efficiency contribution: one-step self-distillation removes the need for per-image diffusion inversion, yielding an 81x inference speedup while improving boundary connectivity.
Introduces a new instance-edge quality benchmark (ODS/OIS/clDice derived from COCO panoptic boundaries) that could be useful to the community beyond this paper.
Honest and detailed limitations analysis (tiny objects in satellite imagery, out-of-distribution medical images) with quantitative failure evidence rather than only qualitative hand-waving.

Generalization study across 10 backbones (5 diffusion, 5 non-diffusion) supports the central claim that the effect is specific to generative diffusion training rather than generic self-attention or model scale.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline is fairly complex (IEP search, ABDiv thresholding with a mean+std heuristic, one-step LoRA self-distillation, Boundary-Guided Propagation with its own IoU threshold), which raises reproducibility and sensitivity concerns; while default hyperparameters are reported as stable, more sensitivity analysis across datasets/classes with very different object statistics would strengthen confidence.

Absolute performance in the unsupervised/tag-supervised settings remains low in absolute terms (e.g., AP^mk around 8-14 on COCO), so while relative gains over baselines are consistent, the practical utility versus fully/weakly supervised methods is still limited; the paper could better contextualize how far this is from being practically deployable.

The method still depends on tag-level or point-level supervision to obtain competitive panoptic segmentation numbers (Table 2), so the 'annotation-free' framing in some sections is a bit stronger than what is literally demonstrated end-to-end for panoptic segmentation.

Some claimed 'objective' comparisons (e.g., swapping conventional edge detectors like Canny/HED/PiDiNet/DiffusionEdge into the BGP pipeline) may be somewhat unfair since these detectors were never designed for the instance-separation task; while this is acknowledged, it slightly overstates the novelty of instance-vs-texture edges as a completely new phenomenon.

Comparisons in Table 1(a)/(b) and Table 12 rely on the authors' own reproduction of several baselines (marked with *), which is reasonable but leaves some residual uncertainty about strict fairness versus originally reported numbers.

The paper would benefit from more discussion of computational cost of the full pipeline (IEP search, distillation training time) relative to baselines beyond the single Table 7 overhead summary, especially for practitioners considering adopting TRACE for new domains.
